summaries.gardner: Chubb fits Rule Breaker investing poorly: it is a disciplined leader in a mature, cyclical industry rather than the top dog in an emerging one, and it is not seen as overvalued. It does have strong, long-tenured management, a record of results and backing from Berkshire Hathaway, which raised its stake in late 2025.
summaries.buffett: Chubb fits Buffett's approach well, which is why Berkshire Hathaway owns a large stake: it is an understandable insurer with disciplined underwriting (2025 combined ratio 85.7%), a growing $172.6B investment float, honest long-serving management and consistent book value growth. At about 12.7 times trailing earnings and 1.84 times book value the price looks reasonable rather than a bargain.
summaries.munger: Chubb matches Munger's preference for a great business run with discipline by rational managers who avoid stupidity, as shown by record 2025 results and steady buybacks. Insurance carries catastrophe and reserving risks that must be thought through backwards, but Chubb's diversified, conservatively reserved book limits the ways it could fail.
summaries.lynch: Chubb is a classic Lynch stalwart: a large, profitable company growing earnings at high single to low double digits, with a 33-year streak of dividend increases and a falling share count. Its P/E of about 12.7 is above its long-term expected earnings growth of about 7.7%, so it is fairly priced rather than a Lynch bargain.
summaries.fisher: Chubb meets several Fisher points: capable, long-tenured management, a strong distribution network, excellent underwriting margins and steady expansion into new markets such as Asian life and consumer insurance. It does not depend on R&D, so Fisher's innovation-focused points fit less well.
summaries.graham: Chubb is large, has been profitable for more than ten years, has raised its dividend for 33 consecutive years and more than tripled diluted EPS from $7.79 in 2020 to $25.68 in 2025. It narrowly misses Graham's price tests: about 15.4 times three-year average EPS and a P/E times P/B of about 23.5, just above the 22.5 limit.
summaries.thiel: Chubb does not fit Thiel's Zero to One framework: it has no proprietary technology that is ten times better, and it competes in a crowded global insurance market rather than a monopoly it created. Its strengths are durability, distribution and execution rather than a unique secret.
summaries.gerstner: Chubb is a profitable, efficiently run company with a growing book value and buybacks, which suits Gerstner's emphasis on discipline and efficiency. It is not a beneficiary of AI or other platform shifts, and revenue growth of 6.5% in 2025 is far below the growth he usually seeks.
summaries.druckenmiller: Chubb's earnings rose strongly in 2025 and analysts raised 2026 estimates, but the commercial insurance cycle is softening, which works against Druckenmiller's focus on businesses that will look better in 18-24 months. Falling interest rates would also slow investment income growth.
summaries.smith: Chubb partly fits Terry Smith's 'buy good companies' test: it earns a 15.0% ROE and 20.5% core operating ROTE (2025) with low leverage and strong cash generation, but insurance is cyclical and capital-intensive, a sector Fundsmith generally avoids. The valuation is reasonable at about 12.7 times earnings.
summaries.greenblatt: On Magic Formula measures Chubb's earnings yield is moderate (pre-tax income about 8.6% of enterprise value) but its return on capital is not comparable to industrial companies because insurers hold large investment portfolios; Greenblatt's screen excludes financial companies like insurers.
summaries.akre: Chubb fits Akre's three-legged stool reasonably: a business with above-average returns (core operating ROTE 20.5%), excellent long-tenured management under Evan Greenberg, and reinvestment through acquisitions and buybacks. Reinvestment runways at high returns are limited by the mature, cyclical nature of insurance.
summaries.pabrai: Chubb offers low risk of permanent loss thanks to a diversified, strongly rated balance sheet, but it is not a heads-I-win, tails-I-don't-lose-much bargain: the shares trade near analysts' average target of $366.78 at 1.84 times book value, with no temporary setback to exploit.
summaries.wood: Chubb does not fit Cathie Wood's disruptive-innovation framework: it is not a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or genomic sequencing, and its market is mature. It is more likely to be affected by insurtech disruption than to drive it.
summaries.ackman: Chubb fits much of Ackman's checklist: a simple, predictable, free-cash-flow-generating business with a strong competitive position, moderate leverage and excellent management. Its exposure to catastrophe losses and the insurance cycle makes earnings less predictable than his ideal.
summaries.sleep: Chubb only partly fits Nick Sleep's scale-economies-shared model: its scale and underwriting expertise produce excellent margins, but it keeps them as profit rather than passing savings to customers through lower prices, and it does not grow like the compounders Sleep favoured.
summaries.valentine: Chubb does not fit Don Valentine's venture approach of backing companies that create huge new markets with new technology; it is a mature incumbent selling a long-established product.
summaries.nash: Chubb fails most of Tom Nash's growth-focused tests: revenue grows below 10% a year, debt exceeds cash and short-term investments, and it is not built around a secular trend, giving a Nash score of about 65. It passes on profitability, earnings beats and a mechanical DCF value well above the price, but that DCF overstates insurer free cash flow.

momentum.evidence: CB rose from about $277 in October 2025 to $359.79 on October 16, 2026 (about 30%), and was up about 13% year to date by July 2026 versus 8.7% for the S&P 500.

g4.evidence: Evan Greenberg has run ACE/Chubb since 2004 and was named one of Barron's Top 25 CEOs of 2026, and Berkshire Hathaway is a major shareholder that increased its position in late 2025.

g6.evidence: Analysts mostly see Chubb as fairly valued: the average price target is $366.78 (25 analysts), close to the $359.79 price, with 14 Hold ratings.

simple.evidence: Chubb collects insurance premiums, pays claims and invests the float, a business a careful generalist can understand, though reserving requires some expertise.

b2.evidence: Net premiums written grew every year from $33.8B in 2020 to $54.8B in 2025 and book value per share rose 18.0% in 2025 to $188.59.

integrity.evidence: Management under Greenberg is known for candid commentary on market conditions (e.g. warning in July 2026 about soft property pricing), returned $4.91B to shareholders in 2025 and has a long record of rational capital allocation.

b6.evidence: Chubb makes regular acquisitions (Chubb Corp 2016, Cigna's Asia business, Huatai stake, Liberty Mutual's Asian operations), but these have been disciplined and complementary rather than empire-building; its pursuit of The Hartford in 2021 was dropped after three rejected offers.

roic.evidence: Chubb earned a 15.0% ROE and 20.5% core operating ROTE in 2025 with debt of only $18.5B against $75.4B of equity (June 2026).

fcf.evidence: Operating cash flow was $12,816M in 2025 against net income of $10,310M, and insurers need little capital spending.

b10.evidence: Book value per share reached $195.45 at June 30, 2026, up from $188.59 at end-2025 after an 18.0% rise in 2025, while the share count fell from 453.4M diluted shares in 2020 to 401.5M in 2025.

safety.evidence: At $359.79 the shares trade at 1.84 times book value and close to the average analyst target of $366.78, so there is no large discount to conservative value.

fairprice.evidence: About 12.7 times trailing GAAP EPS of $28.22 and about 12.8 times 2026 consensus EPS of $28.10 is reasonable for a top-quality insurer earning a 15% ROE.

mu5.evidence: Diversification across 54 countries and many lines limits failure modes, but a mega-catastrophe, major reserve deficiencies or a prolonged soft market could hurt results.

reinvest.evidence: Chubb reinvests through growing premiums, Asian expansion and acquisitions, but premium growth of 6.6% in 2025 shows a mature business that returns much of its capital ($4.91B in 2025).

ly2.evidence: Chubb is a clear stalwart: a large, steadily growing insurer with consistent underwriting profits and dividend increases.

ly3.evidence: The P/E of about 12.7 is above the long-term expected earnings growth rate of about 7.7% (Zacks), giving a PEG above 1.

runway.evidence: Growth in Asian life and consumer insurance and international markets gives a long runway, but core commercial P&C grows near nominal GDP and pricing.

ly7.evidence: The company is shrinking its share count steadily ($3.39B of buybacks in 2025 and $2.12B in the first half of 2026), but there is no evidence of insider open-market buying.

ly8.evidence: Chubb is widely covered by Wall Street (25 analysts) and well known as a top insurer, though insurance is considered a 'boring' industry.

fi2.evidence: Chubb keeps adding coverages such as cyber and digital distribution partnerships, but insurance products evolve slowly.

fi3.evidence: Chubb does not report R&D spending; its technology investment is embedded in administrative costs.

fi4.evidence: Chubb has deep broker and agent relationships plus bank and digital distribution partnerships in Asia and Latin America, and grew net premiums written 6.6% to $54.8B in 2025.

longterm.evidence: Chubb accepts slower growth to keep underwriting discipline, as Greenberg said in July 2026 about the 'growth penalty' it is paying in soft property markets.

gr1.evidence: Chubb is one of the world's largest P&C insurers with $59.4B of 2025 revenue and a market value of about $141B.

ni10.evidence: Chubb has been profitable every year for more than a decade, including $3.5B of net income in the pandemic-hit year 2020.

gr4.evidence: Chubb (formerly ACE) has paid dividends every year since the 1990s and its board recommended a 33rd consecutive annual increase in 2026.

eps10.evidence: Diluted EPS rose from $7.79 in 2020 to $25.68 in 2025, far more than a one-third rise over ten years.

gr6.evidence: The price of $359.79 is about 15.4 times average diluted EPS for 2023-2025 ($23.39), right at Graham's limit.

gr7.evidence: P/E of about 12.7 times P/B of about 1.84 gives about 23.5, slightly above Graham's 22.5 ceiling.

th1.evidence: Chubb has no proprietary technology ten times better than rivals; its edge is underwriting know-how.

timing.evidence: Strong investment income and record margins help now, but commercial insurance pricing is softening in 2026.

th3.evidence: Chubb grew through acquisitions in large, established insurance markets rather than starting from a dominant share of a small market.

team.evidence: Evan Greenberg and his team have a long, distinguished record, including the successful ACE-Chubb merger and record 2025 results.

th5.evidence: Chubb sells through a global network of brokers and agents plus bank, retail and digital partners in 54 countries and territories.

durable.evidence: Insurance demand is permanent and Chubb's scale, ratings and underwriting culture should keep it a leader for decades.

trend.evidence: Chubb is not a leading beneficiary of AI, cloud or another platform shift, though it uses data and digital distribution.

tn21.evidence: No red flags found: a single CEO, disciplined acquisitions, no accounting concerns or auditor change, and margins rising in 2025.

tn22.evidence: Chubb has $59.4B of revenue, strong profits and buys back stock rather than issuing it.
